title: Viral Video Reveals Spiti Monastery Kitchen Where Monks Cook From 1 AM
excerpt: Monk Ten Zin's viral video shows the 1 a.m. kitchen routine inside a Spiti monastery — giant bolep korkun rotis, rotating menus of biryani and fried rice, and teamwork over ceremony.
body:
• Ten Zin, a monk living in Spiti, Himachal Pradesh, shared a viral video showing monks preparing breakfast in a monastery kitchen, with work starting at 1 or 2 in the morning.
  • The monastery's signature flatbread, known as bolep korkun, is far thicker than regular chapatis — Ten Zin jokes a saw would be needed to cut one.
  • The menu changes daily: rotis with vegetables and tea on some mornings, fried rice or biryani on others, and a cheese-filled Tibetan flatbread called chura baklap on special occasions.
  • Kitchen duty rotates, with each monk typically assigned cooking responsibility about twice a month.

Breakfast inside a Buddhist monastery in Spiti starts at 1 in the morning. A viral video by Ten Zin, a monk living in the high Himalayan valley of Himachal Pradesh, has given millions of viewers a look at the communal kitchen where monks cook the day's first meal together — and it is far more hands-on than most people would imagine.

The video shows a busy, unglamorous kitchen: monks chopping vegetables, rolling dough and cooking flatbreads in an assembly line that moves, in one reporter's phrase, like a well-rehearsed team. Each monk handles one task — vegetables, rotis, the main dish — and the meal comes together through sheer coordination.

What do monks eat?

The menu is not the same every day. On some mornings the monks eat freshly cooked rotis with vegetables and tea. On others, the kitchen turns out fried rice or even biryani. For special occasions there is chura baklap, a Tibetan flatbread filled with chura, a type of local cheese.

The real star of the video is the roti itself. Known as bolep korkun, it is dramatically thicker than the regular chapatis most Indians know — Ten Zin has made a separate video about it, leaning into the running joke that the flatbreads are so thick a saw would be needed to cut one. Despite their size, he says, they are easy to tear, and the monks break them into smaller pieces before eating.

"We don't eat the same food every day at our monastery! Simple food, lots of love, and a whole lot of teamwork!"

— Ten Zin, monk and content creator

The 1 a.m. routine

The detail that has surprised viewers most is the hour. According to Ten Zin, breakfast preparation can begin at 1 or 2 in the morning. The work is divided among the monks, who take turns on kitchen duty — each monk is typically assigned the responsibility about twice a month, and the rest of the day is given to classes, study and prayer.

There is nothing performative about the footage. No plated aesthetics, no voiceover philosophy — just vegetables being chopped, dough being rolled, and a team of monks getting on with it. That ordinariness is arguably the point, and the reason the video has travelled.

Why it resonates

Monastic food in the popular imagination tends to fall into two camps: ascetic simplicity or exotic ritual. The Spiti videos quietly correct both. The food is simple, yes — rotis, vegetables, tea — but it is also varied, generous and communal, closer to a large family kitchen than a temple offering. The biryani days and the cheese flatbreads are a reminder that Himalayan monastic cuisine is shaped by place as much as by doctrine.

Ten Zin's account has become one of the most-watched windows into everyday monastic life in India, precisely because it treats the extraordinary as routine.
nri_angle: For diaspora viewers who picture monastic life as pure austerity, the videos offer an affectionate, humanizing glimpse of Himalayan Buddhist kitchen life.
